summary: Specifies how neighboring ATM label switching routers tell each other VCID values for their virtual connections when using LDP. This lets both ends agree on which circuit is which. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3038 solves a naming problem on ATM networks. Because each ATM switch rewrites the labels on a virtual circuit, the two ends of a circuit do not agree on what the circuit is called. This RFC defines a new number, the VCID, that both ends agree on, and the messages that establish it.

questions: how does ldp work over atm
why are vpi and vci not enough for ldp
subtitle: A way to name the same ATM virtual circuit at both ends, so LDP can map labels across it.

tldr.problem: An ATM virtual circuit is labelled with a VPI and a VCI, and every ATM switch in the path rewrites those labels. Because the labels differ at the two ends, they cannot be used to identify a circuit in an LDP label mapping message.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC introduces the Virtual Connection Identifier, a value chosen by the upstream node and agreed with the downstream node through a three-message handshake, and then used in the label TLV of LDP messages.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3038 is a Proposed Standard from January 2001 and has been updated by RFC 7274.

facts.label: Label stack value for an inband propose

today: RFC 3038 is a Proposed Standard from January 2001 and has been updated by RFC 7274. It remains the specification for agreeing VCID values between neighbouring ATM label switching routers.

sections.title: The Problem with ATM Labels
sections.content:
The ATM Label Switching Router is one of the main applications of label switching. In the case of ATM virtual circuits, the VPI and VCI labels are in general rewritten with new values at every switch node the circuit passes through, so they cannot be used to identify a circuit end to end.

In MPLS, a stream is a class of packets that share some characteristic deduced from the layer 3 header, and a stream is bound to a layer 2 label. Those bindings are conveyed between peer label switching routers by the Label Distribution Protocol, defined in RFC 3036. Applying MPLS to ATM links therefore needs a way to identify ATM virtual circuits in LDP mapping messages, and that is what the Virtual Connection Identifier provides. A VCID has the same value at both ends of a circuit.

The RFC specifies the procedures by which neighbouring ATM label switching routers communicate VCID values to each other, which is what makes that shared value true.
sections.plainLanguage: Every ATM switch renumbers the labels on a virtual circuit as it passes, so the label at one end says nothing about the label at the other. The VCID is a separate number that both ends agree on and use in LDP messages.

sections.title: Two Families of Notification Procedure
sections.content:
There are two broad categories of VCID notification procedure, and the difference is which connection the notification messages travel on. In the inband procedures the messages are forwarded over the very circuit they refer to. In the outband procedures the messages travel over some other connection than that circuit.

The RFC works through the link types. A transparent point-to-point link, one where the VPI and VCI are the same at both ends of the circuit, needs no notification at all, because the label already identifies the circuit. For a virtual path, inband notification is used when the VPI differs at the two ends, and a separate VPID notification is used in that case as well. If a node has only one virtual path to a neighbour, no notification is needed, because the VCI is the same at both ends of the path. A permanent virtual circuit uses inband notification, because the labels at each end may differ. A switched virtual circuit has three possibilities: outband notification when the signalling message has a field large enough to carry a VCID, outband notification using a small-sized field when it does not, and inband notification when the signalling message cannot carry user information at all.

The RFC also notes the effect of multicast on the choice. When a label switched path is a point-to-multipoint circuit and the ATM switch in a router cannot merge circuits, adding a new leaf means the active path has to be split temporarily so that an inband notification can be sent.

A circuit has a direction, and the notification is always triggered from the upstream node, which notifies the downstream node of the VCID. If bidirectional use of a label switched circuit is allowed, the circuit is bidirectional and two procedures are performed, one for each direction. If it is not allowed, the circuit is unidirectional and only one procedure is performed, for the allowed direction. The direction is communicated through LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: A notification either travels inside the circuit it is about, which is called inband, or over a different connection, which is called outband. The RFC picks a method for each kind of ATM link, and says the upstream node always starts the exchange.

sections.title: Inband Notification
sections.content:
For a point-to-point circuit, the upstream node A establishes a circuit to the downstream node B, by signalling or by management, and then chooses a VCID value. Node A sends a VCID PROPOSE message through the new circuit, carrying the VCID value and a message ID, and records the association between the outgoing label, that is the VPI and VCI, and the VCID.

Node B receives the message on the circuit and associates the VCID in the message with the incoming label of the circuit. Until node B receives the LDP Request message, it discards any packet that arrives on the circuit other than the VCID PROPOSE message. Node B then sends a VCID ACK message through the circuit, containing the same VCID and message ID it received.

When node A receives the ACK, it checks that the VCID and message ID match the ones it registered. If they match, it treats the association as established; otherwise it ignores the message. If the expected ACK does not arrive within a given period, node A resends the VCID PROPOSE message. After the ACK, node A sends an LDP REQUEST message carrying the message ID used in the proposal. When node B receives that, it treats the exchange as complete, ignores any further VCID PROPOSE messages on that circuit, and sends an LDP Mapping message that carries the VCID value in the label TLV.

The three messages, VCID PROPOSE, VCID ACK and LDP REQUEST, form a three-way handshake. The RFC explains why three are needed: the transmission of the VCID PROPOSE message is unreliable, so the handshake confirms that the proposal really got through and the acknowledgement really came back.

The same idea applies to a point-to-multipoint circuit, where the upstream node assigns the VCID and sends the proposal to all the leaf nodes, which acknowledge it, and the upstream node then sends the LDP REQUEST to complete the handshake. Downstream nodes that have already received the LDP REQUEST for that circuit discard the proposal. The current LDP specification does not support multicast, so this part of the procedure is defined for future use.
sections.plainLanguage: The upstream node picks a number, sends it down the new circuit, and waits for an acknowledgement that repeats the same number and message ID. It then sends an LDP request carrying that ID, which is the third step of the handshake and tells the far end the exchange worked.

sections.title: Outband Notification
sections.content:
Outband notification is used when the circuit is set up by an ATM signalling message and the signalling has a field large enough to carry a VCID value, for example the generic identifier transport. In that case the VCID is carried directly in the signalling message, and afterwards node A sends the LDP request and node B answers with the LDP mapping message containing the VCID in the label TLV.

When the signalling field is too small, the RFC defines an outband procedure using a small-sized field. The SETUP message of the ATM Forum UNI 3.1 and 4.0 signalling has a 7-bit mandatory field for the user, in the layer 3 protocol field of the BLLI information element. The BLLI value is used as a temporary identifier for the circuit during the notification, and it must not be assigned to any other circuit while the procedure is running, so that identifiers do not conflict. Once the association between the BLLI value, a VCID value and the circuit has been established, the BLLI value can be reused. VCID values can be assigned independently of BLLI values.

For a point-to-point circuit, the upstream router establishes the circuit with a BLLI value it is not currently using for any other incomplete transaction with that peer, sends the VCID PROPOSE message through the circuit for LDP to notify the downstream router of the association between the BLLI and VCID values, and the downstream router records that association and answers with an ACK. The upstream router then records the association between the circuit and the VCID, the circuit becomes ready to use, and the BLLI value is free again. The LDP request and mapping follow as usual.

A point-to-multipoint circuit can also be set up with the ADD_PARTY message, which adds a leaf to an existing circuit or tree. The BLLI value in ADD_PARTY has to be the same value that was used to establish the first point-to-point circuit of the tree, and the same BLLI value may be used in different trees only when those trees cannot add a leaf at the same time. The BLLI value used in the signalling must therefore be decided by the root node of the multicast tree.

The RFC adds a caution about BLLI values. A BLLI value is unique at the sending node, but not at the receiving node, because several sending nodes may allocate the same value. The receiver must therefore recognise the BLLI value together with the sender address, and the ATM signalling messages that carry them, SETUP and ADD_PARTY, carry both.
sections.plainLanguage: When the signalling message can hold the number, it carries it directly. When it cannot, the RFC borrows a small field in the signalling as a temporary label for the circuit, and frees it again once the real number is agreed.

sections.title: VPID Notification for Virtual Paths
sections.content:
The same idea applies to a virtual path, where a VPID notification procedure shares one identifier between both ends of the path. A distinct procedure is performed for each direction of each virtual path.

Once the VPID notification is finished for a path, the VCID of a circuit inside that path is constructed from the VPID in the most significant bits and the VCI in the least significant bits. The VCID can then be used by LDP without any further VCID notification.

The message sequence has four steps. The upstream node sends a VPID PROPOSE message. For a bidirectional label switched circuit, both the upstream and the downstream node use VCI 33; for a unidirectional one, the node with the larger LDP identifier uses VCI 33 and the other uses VCI 34. The VCI value 32, which is used for unlabelled packet transfer, is not used for the VPID procedure, so that the same encapsulation can be used for both the VPID procedure and the inband VCID procedure. The downstream node answers with a VPID ACK, the upstream node sends the LDP Label Request, and the downstream node answers with the LDP Label Mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: A whole virtual path can be given one shared number, the VPID. After that, the number of a circuit inside the path is built from the VPID and the circuit's own VCI, so no further negotiation is needed.

sections.title: VCID Message Formats
sections.content:
An LDP VCID message is the LDP fixed header followed by one or more type-length-value fields. A VCID PROPOSE inband message and a VPID PROPOSE message are sent as a null encapsulation packet through the circuit to be used as a label switched path, with only a label stack header before the LDP VCID PDU, and the label value in the label stack entry is 4. The reserved label value is needed because the downstream node may receive the message after it has already received the LDP Label Request message, and must be able to tell the VCID PROPOSE message from other traffic. The other messages are sent as TCP packets, as in LDP itself.

The message type values are 0x0501 for the VCID Propose inband message, 0x0502 for the VCID Propose message, 0x0503 for the VCID ACK message, 0x0504 for the VCID NACK message, 0x0505 for the VPID Propose inband message, 0x0506 for the VPID ACK message and 0x0507 for the VPID NACK message. An LSR sends the ACK when it accepts the proposal and the NACK when it does not.

The proposal and acknowledgement messages carry a four-octet message ID, used to identify the message, and a label TLV. The label TLV holds the VCID value, or the VPID value in the VPID messages, and its type is VCID 0x0203 or VPID 0x0703. The outband VCID PROPOSE message also carries a temporary ID TLV of type 0x0702, whose value is the one taken from the user specific field of the BLLI. The acknowledgement and rejection messages carry a VCID message ID TLV of type 0x0701, whose value is the same as the message ID of the proposal being answered.

The objects themselves are simple. The VCID label TLV, used to encode labels for a link that does not have the same data link label at both ends of a circuit, holds a 4-byte VCID value. The VPID label TLV, used in the VPID notification procedure, holds a 2-byte VPID value.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is an LDP header followed by typed fields. The field that carries the VCID is a label TLV of type 0x0203, and the field that echoes the proposal's message ID is a TLV of type 0x0701.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the document introduces no new security issues beyond those already present in LDP, and that the same mechanisms proposed for LDP may be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here adds a new security problem. The protections that LDP already has are the ones to use.
